name: Jasper
physical: Traditionally linked to stamina and endurance
Associated with a feeling of physical steadiness
Often kept nearby for comfort during stressful times
summary: Jasper is the opaque, earthy chalcedony nicknamed the supreme nurturer, a grounding, protective stone available in countless colors and patterns.
intro: Jasper is an opaque, fine-grained form of microcrystalline quartz colored by up to twenty percent impurities, mostly iron oxides and clay. The result is a staggering range of colors and patterns: brick red, mustard yellow, forest green, brown, blue-grey, with spots, stripes, rings, and landscapes. It takes a good polish and is hard enough for everyday jewelry. Unlike translucent agate, jasper is solid and matte at heart, which is why many people call it a stone of the earth. Hundreds of named varieties exist, usually labeled by the place or pattern where they were found.
history: Jasper has been worked since the Stone Age, when it was chipped into tools and fire strikers, then drilled into beads and carved into seals. Egyptians used red jasper for amulets, and Greek and Roman gem engravers loved its color. The name likely traces to an old Near Eastern word for the stone. Native American peoples valued jasper for pipes, arrowheads and ceremonial objects. Many traditions called it the rain bringer, believing it could summon storms during drought. In medieval lapidaries it was recommended as a protective stone for travelers, and the Book of Revelation places it first in the foundations of the heavenly city.
meaning: Jasper is known in the crystal tradition as the supreme nurturer. Healers link it to the root chakra, with some varieties touching the sacral, and use it to provide steady, supportive energy in times of stress. It is said to restore a feeling of security, help you stay patient through long efforts and bring clarity about what really matters. People carry it when they feel drained, when they must work long hours or when they are looking after others. The wide range of colors lets practitioners choose a type to match their goal: red for energy, green for calm, brown for grounding, yellow for focus. It is a stone of quiet endurance rather than excitement.
howToUse: Carry a tumbled jasper in your pocket during a hard day, or wear it as a bracelet to keep a steady feeling nearby. Place a polished piece on your desk, in your kitchen or by your front door for protective, nurturing energy. Hold it in meditation while breathing slowly and picturing roots going down into the earth. Combine it with other stones in a grid to add stability. A palm stone is useful when you feel anxious in public. Gift a jasper to someone moving house, starting a job or caring for others.
care: Jasper is hard and tolerates water, so rinse it under lukewarm tap water and dry with a soft cloth. Cleanse with smoke, sound, moonlight, burying it in soil or resting on selenite. Sunlight and moonlight are fine for natural stones. Dyed jasper may fade, so test a small piece. Store it separately from harder stones to protect the polish, and avoid harsh chemicals.
identify: Natural jasper is opaque with a dull-to-waxy luster, breaks with a smooth, curved surface and feels cool and dense. Dyed jasper in unnatural blue, purple or neon colors is very common, as is dyed howlite imitation. Glass lookalikes show bubbles and a glassy luster. Because jasper contains so many impurities, look for earthy patterns and natural irregularity, and ask a seller about treatments.

faq.a: Jasper is used for grounding, protection and steady energy. Crystal healers link it to the root chakra and carry it when they want to feel supported, patient and anchored during busy or stressful stretches.

faq.q: What makes jasper different from agate?
faq.a: Both are chalcedony quartz, but jasper is opaque and colored by many impurities, while agate is translucent and banded. Jasper tends to look earthy and solid, whereas agate shows layers and glow.

Yes, jasper is listed as a traditional birthstone for March in some older lists, alongside bloodstone. It is also one of the oldest ornamental stones, used for beads, seals and carvings for millennia.
